extracted.intended_audience: patent practitioners, USPTO Office of Enrollment & Discipline (OED) counsel, and attorneys facing PTO disciplinary review
extracted.subtask_description: Evaluative standards and legal/regulatory criteria used in a USPTO disciplinary proceeding assessing whether a patent practitioner violated PTO disciplinary rules (37 C.F.R. provisions) by neglecting a client matter, failing to inform a client, mishandling client property, or engaging in dishonest or otherwise sanctionable conduct.

rubrics_metrics.name: Neglect (37 C.F.R. § 10.77(c))
rubrics_metrics.description: Neglect occurs when a practitioner ignores or otherwise disregards his obligations to his client. It does not occur instantaneously; neglect generally requires a pattern or course of conduct clearly illustrating the practitioner's disinterest in performing his duties. A single forgetful moment or honest mistake normally will not violate § 10.77(c). Time is a central aspect of the violation.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples and guidance: inaction, delay, and lack of effort (In re Levin). A single negligent act may, in some scenarios, constitute neglect (Attorney Grievance Commission v. Montgomery). The Court found neglect where the practitioner failed to monitor the application, did not return examiner or client calls, ignored client emails for extended periods, and failed to safeguard communications, such that multiple missteps over months/years painted a pattern of neglect. The existence of many small failures spread over time can cumulatively constitute neglect.

rubrics_metrics.name: Timing for continuing violations / accrual
rubrics_metrics.description: For continuing violation theories (e.g., failure to inform), the clock begins when the violation itself ends, not when its impact is felt.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Illustrative application: a failure-to-inform violation was treated as having ended on the date the underlying correspondence was issued; consequences (like the client's inability to appeal) do not alter the accrual date for the continuing violation analysis.

rubrics_metrics.name: Duty to monitor prosecution and maintain avenues to learn status
rubrics_metrics.description: Practitioners have an obligation to monitor the progress of a client's patent application and to take reasonable steps to learn of and act upon PTO correspondence.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Practical measures encouraged (but not strictly required): associate the application with a Customer Number and monitor electronically via PAIR; call the patent examiner; check dockets periodically (e.g., every six months); delegate physical-file checks to an associate. Reliance solely on physical mail and occasional calls is insufficient where other reliable means are available. Failure to adopt available protective measures (e.g., PAIR association) may be evidence of negligence.

rubrics_metrics.name: Duty to inform client of significant PTO correspondence (37 C.F.R. § 10.23(c)(8))
rubrics_metrics.description: A practitioner must inform a client when the practitioner receives correspondence from PTO that could have a significant impact on a pending matter and a reasonable practitioner would believe the client should be notified.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: “Inform” is narrower than mere “notify.” It requires providing the client with the important correspondence (e.g., copies) and a full and accurate explanation of the document's contents, ramifications, deadlines (e.g., non-extendable two-month appeal deadline), and available options. Examples of failures: sending an email that mentions an office action without attaching it, misstating whether claims were allowed or only potentially allowable, failing to mention deadlines or need to rewrite claims. Inadequate explanation that leaves the client with an erroneous impression that no action is needed violates § 10.23(c)(8).

rubrics_metrics.name: Duty to maintain and safeguard means of communication and address of record
rubrics_metrics.description: Practitioners must ensure that they receive and can act on PTO correspondence and client communications by maintaining reliable lines of communication and correct addresses of record.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Avoid foreseeable risks (e.g., entrusting mail to an unattended receptionist without safeguards). Reasonable steps include updating address of record, securing email accounts, using electronic monitoring (PAIR), and ensuring someone will retrieve and act on mail if the practitioner has a virtual office or limited physical presence. Failure to take such steps may be imputed to the practitioner and not excused by third-party mishandling.

rubrics_metrics.name: Duty to seek client's lawful objectives and carry out employment contract (37 C.F.R. § 10.84(a))
rubrics_metrics.description: A practitioner must seek a client's lawful objectives and perform the employment contract; neglectful conduct that derails a client's objectives is sanctionable under § 10.84(a). The PTO's rule emphasizes consequences rather than intent; conduct need not be intentional to violate § 10.84(a).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Even absent an explicit engagement agreement, a practitioner retained to attempt to salvage an application must continue to pursue that objective while attorney of record unless properly and effectively withdrawn. Deliberate abandonment or failure to take available remedial steps (e.g., timely appeal or revival) that thwarts client objectives can constitute a violation, regardless of the practitioner's claimed subjective belief about futility.

rubrics_metrics.name: Proper withdrawal / constructive discharge procedures (37 C.F.R. § 10.40)
rubrics_metrics.description: A practitioner who ceases to act for a client must follow the withdrawal procedures set out in the regulations; self-declared 'constructive discharge' without notice and without following § 10.40 does not relieve the practitioner of responsibility.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: To lawfully cease representation the practitioner must give appropriate notice and comply with regulatory procedures; failing to inform the client or to follow the withdrawal process is effectively abandonment and may support a finding of violation of duties to the client.

rubrics_metrics.name: Gross or disreputable conduct (37 C.F.R. § 10.23(a))
rubrics_metrics.description: Violations of the subsections of § 10.23(c) automatically constitute violations of § 10.23(a) and (b); § 10.23(a) prohibits engaging in gross or disreputable conduct.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The Court treated proven violations of § 10.23(c)(8) (failure to inform) as also violating § 10.23(a). No separate analysis is required where a subsection violation is established. This functions as an aggregator that elevates certain misconduct to gross/disreputable status.

rubrics_metrics.name: Dishonesty/fraud/deceit/misrepresentation (37 C.F.R. § 10.23(b)(4))
rubrics_metrics.description: Prohibition against engaging in conduct involving dishonesty, fraud, deceit, or misrepresentation. To establish a violation based on false statements, evidence must show the practitioner knew the statement was incorrect.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The Court evaluated alleged misrepresentations (e.g., emails stating practitioner had attempted to determine status) against available evidence of receipt of PTO documents. The mailbox rule alone (presumption of receipt) is rebuttable and may be too fragile, by itself, to prove deliberate deceit. Knowledge and intent elements are central to proving § 10.23(b)(4) violations.

rubrics_metrics.name: False or misleading information (37 C.F.R. § 10.23(c)(2)(i))
rubrics_metrics.description: Prohibits the communication of information that the practitioner knows to be incorrect.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Because this subsection contains a knowledge requirement, allegations under § 10.23(c)(2)(i) fail where the practitioner did not actually know the true facts (e.g., genuinely did not know an application had been abandoned). Clear proof of the practitioner's knowledge is necessary.

rubrics_metrics.name: Making a false statement of law or fact (37 C.F.R. § 10.85(a)(5))
rubrics_metrics.description: Prohibits making a false statement of law or fact in PTO proceedings; contains a knowledge element (the practitioner must know the statement is false).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Allegations under § 10.85(a)(5) require proof the practitioner knowingly made false statements. If practitioner lacked actual knowledge of the falsity, the claim fails.

rubrics_metrics.name: Prompt return of client property (37 C.F.R. § 10.112(c)(4))
rubrics_metrics.description: A practitioner must promptly deliver to a client, upon request, any client property in the practitioner's possession that the client is entitled to receive (e.g., the client file).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The client's file is the client's property. Retaining liens or claimed lack of access must be justified; absent legitimate grounds or notice that fees are unpaid, a practitioner must promptly return the file upon request. Practitioners should maintain control of client property (e.g., move files to secure location if personal circumstances threaten access) and use reasonable measures (subpoena duces tecum, associate retrieval) where necessary.

rubrics_metrics.name: Catch-all misconduct provision (37 C.F.R. § 10.23(b)(6))
rubrics_metrics.description: Prohibits 'any other conduct that adversely reflects on the practitioner's fitness to practice before the Office.' The 'other' makes § 10.23(b)(6) a residual provision for conduct not covered by earlier subsections.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Interpretation: conduct that violates § 10.23(b)(1)–(5) should not be redundantly charged under § 10.23(b)(6). The provision is intended to capture distinct misconduct that does not fall under the enumerated categories. Charging strategy and sufficiency of allegations should account for this limitation.

rubrics_metrics.name: Mailbox rule as evidentiary presumption
rubrics_metrics.description: The mailbox rule creates a rebuttable presumption that properly addressed documents placed into the possession of a mail delivery service reach their destination in a reasonable time.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Case citations: Rosenthal v. Walker; Rios v. Nicholson; Lupyan v. Corinthian Colleges. The Court cautions that the mailbox presumption alone may be too fragile to support weighty allegations of dishonest or deliberately misleading conduct without additional corroborating evidence.

rubrics_metrics.name: Distinction between communication failures and diligence in pursuing client objectives
rubrics_metrics.description: A practitioner may fail to communicate adequately with a client while still working diligently on behalf of that client; such communication failures violate § 10.23(c)(8) but do not necessarily constitute a violation of § 10.84(a) (failure to seek client's lawful objectives).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Assessment must separately consider whether (a) the practitioner informed the client sufficiently and (b) the practitioner pursued the client's objectives. Both can be evaluated independently; absence of one does not automatically prove the other.
